        "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), the convention of the Lebesgue interface used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\\ge3$, let $\\Phi$ be the fundamental solution of $-\\Delta$ on $\\mathbb R^n$ normalised by $-\\Delta T_\\Phi=\\delta_0$ ([[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]]), so that for $z\\ne0$\n$$\\Phi(z)=\\frac{|z|^{2-n}}{(n-2)\\omega_{n-1}},\\qquad \\nabla\\Phi(z)=-\\frac{z}{\\omega_{n-1}|z|^n},\\qquad |\\nabla\\Phi(z)|=\\frac{1}{\\omega_{n-1}|z|^{n-1}},$$\nlet $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R^n)$ be real, measurable and zero $\\lambda_n$-almost everywhere outside a closed ball $\\overline B_R(0)=\\{x:|x|\\le R\\}$ of finite radius $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let\n$$Nf(x)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\Phi(x-y)f(y)\\,d\\lambda_n(y)$$\nbe the Newtonian potential ([[def-newtonian-potential]]). Then:\n(a) [Representation and differentiability off the far field] for every $x\\in\\mathbb R^n$ with $|x|>2R$ the integral $\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\nabla\\Phi(x-y)f(y)\\,d\\lambda_n(y)$ is absolutely convergent, the function $Nf$ is differentiable at $x$ with\n$$\\nabla(Nf)(x)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\nabla\\Phi(x-y)f(y)\\,d\\lambda_n(y),$$\nand $x\\mapsto\\nabla(Nf)(x)$ is continuous on the open set $\\{x:|x|>2R\\}$;\n(b) [Decay bound] for every $x$ with $|x|>2R$,\n$$|\\nabla(Nf)(x)|\\le\\frac{2^{n-1}\\|f\\|_1}{\\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1}},\\qquad \\|f\\|_1:=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}|f|\\,d\\lambda_n;$$\n(c) [Scope] the hypothesis is compact support together with $L^1$-integrability; no boundedness of $f$ is assumed, and nothing is asserted at points with $|x|\\le2R$ (where the kernel singularity may meet the support of $f$).",
        "strategy": "Fix $x_0$ with $|x_0|>2R$ and choose $0<\\delta<|x_0|-2R$. On the full open ball $U=B_\\delta(x_0)$, every $y\\in\\overline B_R$ obeys $|x-y|\\ge |x_0|-\\delta-R=:c>0$. Thus both $|\\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\\le c^{2-n}|f(y)|/((n-2)\\omega_{n-1})$ and $|\\partial_i\\Phi(x-y)f(y)|\\le c^{1-n}|f(y)|/\\omega_{n-1}$ hold throughout $U$, outside the single null set on which $f$ may fail to vanish off $\\overline B_R$. Equivalently reset $f$ to zero on that set without changing any integral. The majorants are integrable; the kernel and its coordinate derivatives are continuous off zero and their products with measurable $f$ are measurable ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Restricting to each sufficiently short coordinate interval through any $x\\in U$, [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] yields $\\partial_iNf(x)=\\int\\partial_i\\Phi(x-y)f(y)dy$. For any sequence $x_m\\to x$ in $U$, the derivative integrands converge almost everywhere and have the same full-neighbourhood majorant $c^{1-n}|f|/\\omega_{n-1}$. [[thm-dominated-convergence]] therefore proves continuity of each partial derivative as a function of all coordinates on $U$, not merely along coordinate lines. [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]] now gives total differentiability and the displayed gradient representation; the continuous vector of partials is the gradient ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). As $x_0$ was arbitrary, (a) holds throughout the stated far field. For (b), $|x-y|\\ge |x|-R>|x|/2$ on the support, so $|\\nabla\\Phi(x-y)|\\le2^{n-1}/(\\omega_{n-1}|x|^{n-1})$; integrating against $|f|$ gives the stated bound. No boundedness of $f$ or interior-support assertion is used. The support ball is measurable, and the choice cost is exactly the declared $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$ of the measure interfaces.",

        "inventory_expansion_required": false,
        "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$) for the Lebesgue and product-measure interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\\ge2$, let $p\\in\\mathbb R^n$, and let $u\\in L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}(\\mathbb R^n)$ be continuous on $\\mathbb R^n\\setminus\\{p\\}$ and of class $C^1$ there, with each classical partial derivative $\\partial_iu:\\mathbb R^n\\setminus\\{p\\}\\to\\mathbb R$ (extended by $0$ at $p$) again in $L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}(\\mathbb R^n)$. Then for every $i=1,\\dots,n$, with $T_u\\in\\mathcal D'(\\mathbb R^n)$ the regular distribution of $u$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\\partial_i$ the distributional derivative ([[def-distributional-derivative]]),\n$$\\partial_iT_u=T_{\\partial_iu}\\qquad\\text{in }\\mathcal D'(\\mathbb R^n),$$\nthat is, $\\langle\\partial_iT_u,\\psi\\rangle=\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\partial_iu\\,\\psi\\,d\\lambda_n$ for every $\\psi\\in C_c^\\infty(\\mathbb R^n)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). The value assigned to $\\partial_iu$ at the single point $p$ is immaterial, because a singleton is Lebesgue null ([[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Both hypotheses are used: $u$ must be locally integrable and continuous away from $p$, and each classical partial must be locally integrable; the lemma is asserted for one exceptional point, not for an exceptional set of positive surface measure.",
        "strategy": "The given $u$ is continuous off $p$, hence Borel there; assigning a finite value at $p$ makes a Borel representative on all of $\\mathbb R^n$. Each classical partial is continuous off $p$ and is extended by zero there, hence is also Borel. Thus the products with tests below are Borel, so the cited Borel product-measure identification applies directly. Fix $i$ and $\\psi\\in C_c^\\infty(\\mathbb R^n)$; both $\\partial_iu\\,\\psi$ and $u\\,\\partial_i\\psi$ are integrable on $\\mathbb R^n$: for the first, $|\\partial_iu\\,\\psi|\\le\\|\\psi\\|_\\infty|\\partial_iu|$ with $\\partial_iu\\in L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}$ and $\\psi$ compactly supported, and for the second $|u\\,\\partial_i\\psi|\\le\\|\\partial_i\\psi\\|_\\infty|u|$ with $u\\in L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}$ ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]). Split $\\mathbb R^n=\\mathbb R\\times\\mathbb R^{n-1}$ into the $i$-th coordinate $t$ and the remaining coordinates $y$; identify the Lebesgue measure with the product measure ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]], [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]], [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]), so that [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] applies to both integrable functions. Let $Y$ be the set of $y$ for which the line $\\{(t,y):t\\in\\mathbb R\\}$ meets $p$: it is the single transverse point $y=p'$, a $\\lambda_{n-1}$-null set by [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]] (this is where $n\\ge2$ is used: for $n=1$ there are no transverse coordinates and the case would have to be argued separately by absolute continuity). For every $y\\notin Y$ the line misses $p$, so $t\\mapsto u(t,y)$ is $C^1$ on $\\mathbb R$ with derivative $t\\mapsto\\partial_iu(t,y)$, and $t\\mapsto u(t,y)\\psi(t,y)$ is $C^1$ with compact support; [[thm-integration-by-parts]] (equivalently the fundamental theorem, [[thm-ftc-first-part]]) on an interval containing the support gives\n$$\\int_{\\mathbb R}\\partial_iu(t,y)\\psi(t,y)\\,dt=-\\int_{\\mathbb R}u(t,y)\\partial_i\\psi(t,y)\\,dt.$$\nThis holds for every $y\\notin Y$, hence almost everywhere. Fubini's theorem applied to the two integrable functions gives\n$$\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}\\partial_iu\\,\\psi\\,d\\lambda_n=\\int_{\\mathbb R^{n-1}}\\!\\!\\int_{\\mathbb R}(\\partial_iu\\,\\psi)\\,dt\\,dy=-\\int_{\\mathbb R^{n-1}}\\!\\!\\int_{\\mathbb R}(u\\,\\partial_i\\psi)\\,dt\\,dy=-\\int_{\\mathbb R^n}u\\,\\partial_i\\psi\\,d\\lambda_n.$$\nThe right-hand side is $-\\langle T_u,\\partial_i\\psi\\rangle=\\langle\\partial_iT_u,\\psi\\rangle$ by the definition of the distributional derivative ([[def-distribution]]), and the left-hand side is $\\langle T_{\\partial_iu},\\psi\\rangle$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Hence $\\partial_iT_u=T_{\\partial_iu}$. Measurability of $\\partial_iu$ is not assumed beyond the stated $L^1_{\\mathrm{loc}}$ membership of its extension: on $\\mathbb R^n\\setminus\\{p\\}$ it is the pointwise limit of the difference quotients of the measurable $u$, hence measurable there by the closure properties of measurable functions ([[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and the single point $p$ does not affect the classes ([[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]). The splitting, the identification of the product measure and the two Fubini applications are the only measure-theoretic inputs; the choice cost is the declared $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately.",

        "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces used below ([[def-countable-choice]]). On $\\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) let $0<\\varepsilon<R$ and put\n$$B_R:=\\{x:|x|<R\\},\\qquad \\overline B_R:=\\{x:|x|\\le R\\},\\qquad A_{\\varepsilon,R}:=\\{x:\\varepsilon<|x|<R\\},\\qquad S_r:=\\{x:|x|=r\\}.$$\nThen:\n(a) [Domains] $B_R$ and $A_{\\varepsilon,R}$ are bounded $C^1$ domains in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; their boundaries are $S_R$, respectively $S_\\varepsilon\\cup S_R$, and the corresponding outward unit normals are\n$$\\nu(x)=\\frac{x}{|x|}\\ \\ (x\\in S_R),\\qquad \\nu(x)=-\\frac{x}{|x|}\\ \\ (x\\in S_\\varepsilon,\\ \\text{boundary of }A_{\\varepsilon,R});$$\n(b) [Spheres] each $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ (indeed $C^\\infty$) hypersurface in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] with two-sided unit normals $\\pm x/|x|$, and the boundary components $S_\\varepsilon,S_R$, each subdivided into six compact signed-maximal-coordinate graph faces $F_{r,k,\\sigma}:=\\{x\\in S_r:\\sigma x_k\\ge |x_j|\\text{ for all }j\\}$ ($k=1,2,3$, $\\sigma=\\pm1$), with the compact edge set consisting of their seams $\\sigma x_k=|x_j|$ for $j\\ne k$, give a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of $A_{\\varepsilon,R}$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]];\n(c) [Consequences used downstream] the divergence theorem and Green's first identity of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] and [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] apply on $B_R$ and on $A_{\\varepsilon,R}$ with the outward normals of (a), and $S_r$ carries a finite Borel surface measure with the standard graph charts.",
        "strategy": "The continuous norm makes $B_R$ and $A_{\\varepsilon,R}$ nonempty bounded open sets, and radial perturbations show their boundaries are respectively $S_R$ and $S_\\varepsilon\\cup S_R$ ([[thm-continuity-preimage-characterisation]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]]). Here is an explicit finite graph cover of a sphere $S_r$. For $k=1,2,3$ and $\\sigma\\in\\{+1,-1\\}$ use the relatively open patch $\\sigma x_k>r/(2\\sqrt3)$; these six patches cover because some $|x_k|\\ge r/\\sqrt3$. In rigid coordinates $(y,z)$ with $z=\\sigma x_k$, each patch lies on the positive graph $z=h(y)=\\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$. Around each point choose a graph cylinder small enough that $z>0$, $|y|<r$ and any other annulus boundary is absent. The sphere is exactly this graph, and the ball is exactly $z<h(y)$ there. In particular reflection of a lower physical hemisphere yields the positive graph $+\\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$, not the negative graph. The chain and power rules make $h$ smooth on $|y|<r$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]). For the inner boundary of the annulus the domain is locally the complement of $\\overline B_\\varepsilon$. Starting with $z=\\sigma x_k>0$, reflect once more to $w=-z$; the graph is $w=-h(y)$ and the exterior condition $z>h(y)$ becomes exactly the required subgraph $w<-h(y)$. The outer boundary uses the ball chart. The definition's graph normal $(-Dh,1)/\\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, with $Dh=-y/h$, transports to $x/r$ for the ball/outer sphere. For the complement chart $g=-h$, its graph normal is $(-Dg,1)/\\sqrt{1+|Dg|^2}=(-y,h)/r$ in $(y,w)$; transport by $w=-\\sigma x_k$ gives $-x/r$, the annulus inner normal. Hence (a) and its signs follow from [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Each sphere is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], and the six smooth graph patches make it a compact embedded smooth hypersurface with two-sided normals. For the finite piecewise presentation, subdivide each sphere component into the six compact Borel faces $F_{r,k,\\sigma}$ of (b). They cover $S_r$. On each face $\\sigma x_k\\ge r/\\sqrt3$, so the whole face is contained in the one regular positive graph patch $z=\\sigma x_k=\\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$ with $z>r/(2\\sqrt3)$. The parameter set of that face is compactly contained in $|y|<r$. Define $E$ to be the finite union, for $r=\\varepsilon,R$, of the seams where two or more coordinates have tied maximal absolute value. This is compact and contains every relative face boundary and every distinct-face overlap. In the chart of $F_{r,k,\\sigma}$ any seam is contained in $h(y)=|y_j|$ for one of the two other coordinates $j$, hence satisfies $y_j=\\pm\\sqrt{(r^2-y_\\ell^2)/2}$ with $\\ell\\ne j,k$. For each fixed $y_\\ell$ this has at most two $y_j$ values, so its Borel parameter set has planar Lebesgue measure zero by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]. Its chart density $\\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ is bounded on the compact face, so it also has zero chart surface measure by [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] and [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. Away from $E$ the already established smooth domain chart is a single graph and the normals are exactly the outward ones computed above. These twelve faces and their null seam set satisfy every requirement of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]. The divergence theorem and first Green identity apply to these domains with precisely those normals ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]], [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). The compact chart surface carries finite Borel measure by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. The only choice cost is the declared $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$ of that interface.         "statement": "Let $\\gamma:[0,L]\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length ($|\\gamma'|\\equiv1$) that is either closed ($\\gamma(0)=\\gamma(L)$ with matching one-sided derivatives) or a wire segment with free endpoints, let $I\\in\\mathbb R$, let $m=\\frac I2\\int_0^L\\gamma(s)\\times\\gamma'(s)\\,ds$ be the finite Riemann source moment defined by this displayed integral in the closed case. For an embedded closed loop this agrees with [[def-em-magnetic-moment]](b); embeddedness is not required for the present parametrized-curve calculation. Let $B$ be a prescribed external magnetic field, of class $C^0$ on a neighbourhood of the trace of $\\gamma$ in part (a) and of class $C^2$ on an open set containing the closed ball $\\overline{B_a(0)}$ in parts (b)-(d). Adopt the thin-wire coupling hypothesis (W): for a general closed parametrized curve use the stated direct neutral-wire Riemann coupling (with multiplicity of traversal retained); in the embedded closed-loop specialization its source interpretation is exactly [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1); for an open curve use a compact segment of a fed or closed neutral circuit, including a segment of the declared infinite wire of (c2). Adopt separately for that parametrized wire or local segment the direct external magnetic coupling $dF=I\\,d\\gamma\\times B$ and $dN=\\gamma\\times dF$, as an ideal extension motivated by the smooth continuum Lorentz law [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii); that smooth-source postulate does not itself include singular currents. An isolated static neutral open segment is not asserted: its standalone current satisfies $\\operatorname{div}J_{\\rm seg}=I(\\delta_{\\gamma(0)}-\\delta_{\\gamma(L)})$, so its endpoint feed/return cannot be suppressed in a global model.         "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no other choice principle is used. Let $k\\ge1$ and let $D\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (nonempty, bounded, open, and locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph function over a hyperplane). Then:\n(a) [Compactness and finiteness] $\\partial D$ is nonempty and compact; the complement $\\mathbb R^3\\setminus\\partial D$ need not be connected here. Moreover $\\partial D$ has finitely many connected components, and each connected component of $\\partial D$ is compact.\n(b) [Finite embedded presentation] the local boundary charts give finitely many regular injective $C^k$ parametrisations of $\\partial D$ with $C^k$ coordinate transitions, of the graph type required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]: writing a chart as $R(p)=(y,s)$, the graph map $y\\mapsto R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective, of class $C^k$, with $C^k$ inverse (the inverse is $p\\mapsto\\pi(R(p))$ restricted to the graph, where $\\pi(y,s)=y$); consequently $\\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface, and for $k\\ge1$ it carries the finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]].\n(c) [Normal field] the outward unit normal $\\nu$ of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a continuous unit normal field on $\\partial D$, with $\\nu(x)$ orthogonal to the tangent plane of the graph chart at each $x$; it is the field used by the Green and divergence items cited by this page's consumers.\nThe statement is geometric: it asserts no differentiability of $D$ beyond $C^k$, no boundedness of chart derivatives beyond the compact patches, and no connectedness of either $D$ or $\\partial D$.",
        "strategy": "The boundary is nonempty: otherwise the nonempty open bounded $D$ would also be closed and disconnect connected $\\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], [[cor-rn-is-polygonally-connected-and-locally-path-connected]], [[thm-path-connected-implies-connected]]). It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. At every boundary point first shrink its graph chart to the inverse image of a small flattening cylinder $B'\\times(-b,b)$ with $\\overline{B'}$ compactly contained in the original parameter ball. Its boundary patch is exactly the graph $X(y)=R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ over the connected ball $B'$. The graph is homeomorphic to $B'$ by the coordinate projection, so is a connected relatively open neighbourhood in $\\partial D$. Arbitrarily small such graph neighbourhoods prove local connectedness of $\\partial D$ directly; local connectedness is not inherited by arbitrary Euclidean subspaces. A component is open because each of these connected neighbourhoods meeting it lies in it by maximality; it is closed because the closure of a connected set is connected (if separated, the two relative open separating sets would also separate the dense original connected set). Compactness and the open component cover therefore give finitely many components, each closed and compact. For the embedded presentation, the graph maps are injective and $C^k$, and their derivatives have independent tangent columns since projection onto $y$ has derivative the identity; their inverses are the restricted coordinate projections. Transitions are the corresponding projections composed with the graph maps and rigid motions, hence $C^k$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Choose these smaller chart neighbourhoods at every point first, and only then take a finite subcover of the compact boundary. The associated larger charts provide room for compact supports of a subordinate partition; their graph densities and derivatives are bounded on those compact supports. This supplies exactly the finite compact embedded hypersurface and finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. The outward graph normal is the continuous $(-Dh,1)/\\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ transported by the rigid coordinates; overlap agreement is supplied by [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. No domain or boundary connectedness is assumed, and the only choice assumption used is the declared $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$.",

        "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$) as carried by the boundary interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $k\\ge1$, let $\\Omega\\subset\\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain, and let $D_1,\\dots,D_m$ ($m\\ge0$) be bounded $C^k$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures whose closures satisfy $\\overline{D_1}\\cup\\cdots\\cup\\overline{D_m}\\subset\\Omega$ strictly inside $\\Omega$. Put\n$$\\Omega_v:=\\Omega\\setminus\\bigl(\\overline{D_1}\\cup\\cdots\\cup\\overline{D_m}\\bigr).$$\nThen:\n(a) [Domain] $\\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (in particular nonempty, bounded and open);\n(b) [Boundary] $\\partial\\Omega_v=\\partial\\Omega\\cup\\partial D_1\\cup\\cdots\\cup\\partial D_m$, a disjoint union of nonempty compact sets; the compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurfaces $\\partial\\Omega,\\partial D_1,\\dots,\\partial D_m$ are pairwise disjoint ([[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]);\n(c) [Normals and sign] the outward unit normal of $\\Omega_v$ at a point of $\\partial\\Omega$ equals the outward unit normal of $\\Omega$, and at a point of $\\partial D_j$ it equals the negative of the outward unit normal of $D_j$ defined by [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] and [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; so the outward normal of $\\Omega_v$ on $\\partial D_j$ points from the vacuum into the conductor;\n(d) [Componentwise statement] $\\Omega_v$ has finitely many connected components. Each component $U$ is an open bounded $C^k$ domain; its boundary is the compact restricted subset $\\partial U\\subseteq\\partial\\Omega_v$, a union of the boundary components incident to $U$. The normal formulas in (c) restrict to those boundary pieces. It need not have every boundary piece of $\\Omega_v$, and connectedness of $\\Omega_v$ is not asserted.\nNo regularity beyond $C^k$, no convexity and no topological simplicity is claimed.",
        "strategy": "Let $K=\\bigcup_j\\overline D_j$. It is compact, contained in open $\\Omega$, and its constituent closures are pairwise disjoint. For $m=0$, $K=\\varnothing$. Thus $\\Omega_v=\\Omega\\setminus K$ is open and bounded. It is nonempty: choose a boundary point of nonempty bounded $\\Omega$ by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]; a small neighbourhood of that point avoids compact $K$ and contains interior points of $\\Omega$. At an outer boundary point shrink the $\\Omega$ graph cylinder to avoid $K$; locally the vacuum is the same subgraph as $\\Omega$. At a point of $\\partial D_j$ shrink the $D_j$ chart cylinder to lie inside $\\Omega$ and avoid every other closed body. Precisely $\\Omega_v\\cap W=W\\setminus\\overline D_j$, not $W\\setminus D_j$: in graph coordinates its inequality is strictly $s>h(y)$. Reflection $w=-s$ makes this the subgraph $w<-h(y)$ with $C^k$ graph. These local charts also show $\\partial\\Omega_v=\\partial\\Omega\\sqcup\\bigsqcup_j\\partial D_j$, since the disjoint compact closures prevent other bodies from hiding or touching any boundary piece. The outward normal is the outer-domain normal on $\\partial\\Omega$, and its negative on $\\partial D_j$, because the latter vacuum chart is the exterior of the body. The graph-normal formula in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] verifies this sign. All boundary pieces are compact smooth hypersurfaces by [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]. For components, every point of the open vacuum has a connected open ball inside it; hence its connected component is open. Every boundary point of a component lies on $\\partial\\Omega_v$: a connected ball inside $\\Omega_v$ cannot meet two components. Choose a small flattened cylinder at such a boundary point whose vacuum half-cylinder is connected. Because that half-cylinder meets the component, all of it lies in the component; its graph is therefore the component's local boundary. Thus the component is a bounded $C^k$ domain with the inherited normal on the restricted boundary. A finite cover of compact $\\partial\\Omega_v$ by such connected one-sided graph cylinders meets only finitely many vacuum components. Every nonempty bounded open component has a boundary point, so there are only finitely many components. A boundary component of $\\Omega_v$ is incident to a single vacuum component: the incident component is locally constant along each connected graph boundary patch, hence constant along that boundary component. Consequently each $\\partial U$ is a union of the incident compact boundary components, not necessarily the entire displayed disjoint union. None of these conclusions asserts vacuum connectedness. The corrected separation hypothesis excludes tangent bodies: two tangent balls have disjoint open interiors but a touching point of their closures does not admit the asserted disjoint single-boundary chart.",

        "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $\\theta_0\\in I$, and let $f:I\\to\\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on $I$ in the sense that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ and $f'$ is continuous on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]). Let a recorded scalar $\\hat y\\in\\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\\hat y|\\le s$ with $s\\ge0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), and let a separately specified calibration-error model bound be $|y-\\hat y|\\le\\delta$ with $\\delta\\ge0$ for a value $y$ assigned to the same quantity.         "statement": "Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).     "statement": "Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$), the convention of the test-geometry and divergence-theorem items cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Then, for every $t\\in I$:\n\n(a) [Total current flux is surface independent]\n$$\\int_{S_1}\\bigl(J+\\varepsilon_0\\partial_tE\\bigr)(\\cdot,t)\\cdot n_1\\,dS=\\int_{S_2}\\bigl(J+\\varepsilon_0\\partial_tE\\bigr)(\\cdot,t)\\cdot n_2\\,dS=\\frac{1}{\\mu_0}\\oint_\\gamma B(\\cdot,t)\\cdot d\\mathbf r,$$\nwhere $S_i=r_i[D]$ and the flux is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].\n\n(b) [Conduction-only flux need not be] For every $t\\in I$ the difference of the conduction fluxes equals the negative of the difference of the displacement fluxes:\n$$\\int_{S_1}J(\\cdot,t)\\cdot n_1\\,dS-\\int_{S_2}J(\\cdot,t)\\cdot n_2\\,dS=-\\varepsilon_0\\left(\\int_{S_1}\\partial_tE(\\cdot,t)\\cdot n_1\\,dS-\\int_{S_2}\\partial_tE(\\cdot,t)\\cdot n_2\\,dS\\right).$$\nHence the conduction-only fluxes are equal exactly when the displacement fluxes are equal, and neither conclusion is forced by the Maxwell equations alone.\n\n(c) [Explicit realisation] The following declared smooth data satisfies all the hypotheses above and has different conduction fluxes through the two surfaces. On $\\Omega=\\mathbb R^3$, $I=\\mathbb R$, fix $\\chi\\in C^\\infty(\\mathbb R)$ with $0\\le\\chi\\le1$, $\\chi(z)=1$ for $z\\le-1$ and $\\chi(z)=0$ for $z\\ge0$, and set\n$$E(x,t):=\\frac{t}{\\varepsilon_0}\\chi(z)\\,e_z,\\qquad B:=0,\\qquad \\rho(x,t):=t\\,\\chi'(z),\\qquad J(x,t):=-\\chi(z)\\,e_z.$$\nThen $\\operatorname{div}E=\\rho/\\varepsilon_0$, $\\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\\operatorname{curl}E=0=-\\partial_tB$, $\\operatorname{curl}B=0=\\mu_0J+c^{-2}\\partial_tE$ (the last identity because $c^{-2}\\varepsilon_0^{-1}=\\mu_0$), and $\\partial_t\\rho+\\operatorname{div}J=0$. Take $D=[-1,1]^2$ and its interior $D^\\circ=(-1,1)^2$. Let $\\sigma$ be the standard smooth step of [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] and define $h(s):=\\sigma(2(1-s^2))$, $\\eta(u,v):=h(u)h(v)$. Then $\\eta\\in C_c^\\infty(\\mathbb R^2)$, $0\\le\\eta\\le1$, $\\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, $\\eta>0$ at every point of $D^\\circ$, and $\\eta=0$ on $\\partial D$ and outside $D$. Take the graphs\n$$r_1(u,v):=(u,v,-2\\eta(u,v)),\\qquad r_2(u,v):=(u,v,0).$$\nBoth induced boundary chains are the square $\\{(u,v,0):(u,v)\\in\\partial D\\}$, the region $V=\\{(u,v,w):(u,v)\\in D^\\circ,\\ -2\\eta(u,v)<w<0\\}$ is enclosed between the patches, and\n$$\\int_{S_1}J\\cdot n_1\\,dS=-\\int_D\\chi(-2\\eta(u,v))\\,dudv<0,\\qquad \\int_{S_2}J\\cdot n_2\\,dS=-\\int_D\\chi(0)\\,dudv=0,$$\nthe first inequality because $\\eta=1$ in a neighbourhood of the origin, so $\\chi(-2\\eta)=1$ on a nonempty open subset of $D$, whose area is positive.\nwhile both total current fluxes in (a) vanish, consistently with the loop integral $\\oint_\\gamma B\\cdot d\\mathbf r=0$. In the standard charging-capacitor discussion the two spanning surfaces cut the conduction current in different ways and the difference is carried by the displacement term; the realisation above exhibits exactly this phenomenon in a self-contained smooth model. An idealised thin-wire current is not a source type of this framework and the capacitor interpretation is explanatory, not an additional empirical claim.",
    "strategy": "(a) Put $G:=J+\\varepsilon_0\\partial_tE$, of class $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\\overline V$. By the smooth Gauss law and [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], $\\operatorname{div}G=\\operatorname{div}J+\\varepsilon_0\\partial_t\\operatorname{div}E=\\operatorname{div}J+\\partial_t\\rho=0$ on that neighbourhood, the last equality being continuity, [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]](a). [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]] applied to $G$ on the specified presentation of $V$ \u2014 outward normal $-n_1$ on the face $S_1$ and $+n_2$ on the face $S_2$ \u2014 gives $0=\\int_V\\operatorname{div}G=\\int_{S_2}G\\cdot n_2-\\int_{S_1}G\\cdot n_1$, which is the first asserted equality. The equality with $(1/\\mu_0)\\oint_\\gamma B\\cdot d\\mathbf r$ is Ampere's integral identity of [[pthm-em-integral-maxwell]](a) applied to either patch, whose induced boundary chain is $\\gamma$; the two patches consequently give the same circulation. (b) Split $G$ in the equality of (a); this is algebra with the definitions of the fluxes ([[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]) and no further analytic input. (c) Verify the smooth equations for the displayed data by direct substitution: $\\operatorname{div}E=(t/\\varepsilon_0)\\chi'(z)$ and $\\operatorname{div}B=0$; $\\operatorname{curl}E=\\operatorname{curl}(E_z(z,t)e_z)=0$ because $E_z$ is independent of $x$ and $y$, so $\\operatorname{curl}E=-\\partial_tB=0$; $\\operatorname{curl}B=0$ and $\\mu_0J+c^{-2}\\partial_tE=-\\mu_0\\chi(z)e_z+c^{-2}\\varepsilon_0^{-1}\\chi(z)e_z=0$ since $\\varepsilon_0=(\\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$; and $\\partial_t\\rho+\\operatorname{div}J=\\chi'(z)-\\chi'(z)=0$. The standard step is smooth, is zero for arguments at most zero, is one for arguments at least one and is strictly positive on $(0,1)$ ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]]). Thus $h$ is smooth, positive for $|s|<1$, one for $|s|\\le1/\\sqrt2$ and zero for $|s|\\ge1$; the product $\\eta$ has exactly the declared properties. In particular the entire open square has positive graph separation, rather than merely a central subregion. Both graph maps are smooth and injective regular parametrizations on a neighbourhood of $D$, since their first two coordinates are $(u,v)$ and their area vectors are $(-\\varphi_u,-\\varphi_v,1)$. Their induced square boundary chains coincide at height zero. The explicitly restricted $V$ is nonempty, bounded and open, with compact closure contained in $[-1,1]^2\\times[-2,0]$; its boundary is exactly $S_1\\cup S_2$. Strict positivity of $\\eta$ on $D^\\circ$ gives $S_1\\cap S_2=\\partial D\\times\\{0\\}$. This square seam is a compact union of four line segments, has surface measure zero on each regular graph face, and contains the relative face boundaries. At every point off the seam the boundary is locally the single smooth graph with $V$ above the lower graph and below the upper graph. The faces therefore give the actual finite presentation of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]], with outward normals $-n_1,+n_2$, without overlapping positive-area face pieces. For $\\varphi_1=-2\\eta$, the induced upward unit normal is $n_1=(2\\eta_u,2\\eta_v,1)/\\sqrt{1+4|\\nabla\\eta|^2}$, so $(J\\circ r_1)\\cdot n_1=-\\chi(-2\\eta)/\\sqrt{1+4|\\nabla\\eta|^2}$; after multiplication by its area Jacobian the pullback density is $(J\\circ r_1)\\cdot(r_{1,u}\\times r_{1,v})=-\\chi(-2\\eta)$. For the plane $n_2=e_z$ and the density is $-\\chi(0)=0$. The graph flux formula thus gives exactly the two stated integrals, with the unit-normal scalar distinguished from the unnormalized area-vector density. On any ball $B(0,r)$ with $0<r<1/2$, $\\eta=1$ and $\\chi(-2\\eta)=1$. The nonnegative continuous integrand has strictly positive integral on $D$, by the Riemann/Lebesgue comparison, monotonicity and positive ball area already declared; its negative is the strictly negative lower conduction flux, as stated. The total fluxes both vanish because $G=J+\\varepsilon_0\\partial_tE=-\\chi(z)e_z+\\chi(z)e_z=0$, consistent with the vanishing circulation of $B=0$. The explicit step-product supplies the required positivity on the entire square interior; the marked $\\mathrm{AC}_\\omega$ is the convention of the test-geometry, surface-measure and divergence-theorem items, and no further choice is used.",
